pharm: An irreversible beta-lactamase inhibitor that has minimal intrinsic antibacterial activity and is combined with a beta-lactam to protect it from enzymatic hydrolysis and restore activity against beta-lactamase-producing organisms
tags: Not FDA-approved as a single agent
quick: Given with a beta-lactam; e.g. ampicillin/sulbactam 1.5-3 g IV/IM every 6 h (max 4 g sulbactam/day)
Use only if clearly needed; safety in pregnancy not fully established
Small amounts excreted in milk; use with caution
Reduce frequency in significant renal impairment (sulbactam is renally cleared)
No specific adjustment for sulbactam alone; monitor with hepatic dysfunction
Renal/hepatic/hematologic function in prolonged use; signs of hypersensitivity and superinfection
summary: Sulbactam is an irreversible beta-lactamase inhibitor (a penicillanic acid sulfone) with little intrinsic antibacterial activity of its own. It is used as a combination partner with beta-lactam antibiotics (most commonly ampicillin, and outside the US cefoperazone) to protect the partner antibiotic from beta-lactamase-mediated hydrolysis and extend its spectrum to many beta-lactamase-producing bacteria, including Acinetobacter species. Sulbactam alone is not FDA-approved; dosing, indications, and safety derive from the licensed fixed-dose combinations.
indications: Beta-lactamase inhibitor combined with a beta-lactam antibiotic (e.g. ampicillin) for skin/soft tissue, intra-abdominal, and gynecologic infections caused by beta-lactamase-producing organisms
Component of combinations (e.g. cefoperazone/sulbactam, ampicillin/sulbactam) for respiratory, urinary, and other infections per regional labeling
Used (off-label/per regional guidance, often high-dose) against multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii

dosage.d: 1.5 g to 3 g of the combination (containing 0.5-1 g sulbactam) IV or IM every 6 hours
dosage.n: Maximum recommended sulbactam component is 4 g/day

dosage.d: Lengthen the dosing interval of the combination according to creatinine clearance
dosage.t: Reduced frequency (e.g. every 12-24 h in severe impairment)
dosage.n: Sulbactam pharmacokinetics parallel the penicillin partner and are altered by renal impairment

dosage.d: Dose based on the combination (commonly 150 mg/kg/day of ampicillin/sulbactam) in divided doses
dosage.n: Use per the licensed combination product labeling

admin: Administer parenterally (IV infusion/bolus or deep IM injection) as the licensed beta-lactam/sulbactam combination
For IV, reconstitute and dilute per the combination product instructions and infuse over the recommended time
For IM, may be reconstituted with lidocaine to reduce injection pain where permitted
Adjust dosing interval in renal impairment
Sulbactam is not used as a single agent in standard practice; pair with an appropriate beta-lactam
moa: Sulbactam is an irreversible inhibitor of many bacterial beta-lactamases. It has only weak intrinsic antibacterial activity (with some intrinsic activity against Acinetobacter and Neisseria), but by binding and inactivating beta-lactamase enzymes it protects the co-administered beta-lactam antibiotic from hydrolysis, thereby restoring or extending its activity against beta-lactamase-producing strains.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to sulbactam, penicillins, or the partner beta-lactam
History of severe immediate hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis) to any beta-lactam
relative: History of allergy, especially to multiple allergens
Infectious mononucleosis (increased risk of rash with ampicillin combinations)
monitor: Renal, hepatic and hematologic function during prolonged therapy
Signs of hypersensitivity, Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea, and superinfection

preg: Sulbactam (as part of combinations) crosses the placenta. Safety in human pregnancy has not been fully established; reproduction studies have not shown harm but data are limited. Use during pregnancy only when clearly needed and the expected benefit outweighs potential risk, per the partner beta-lactam's pregnancy guidance.
lact: Low concentrations of sulbactam are excreted in human milk. Although generally considered compatible, use with caution and monitor the breastfed infant for diarrhea, candidiasis, or rash, per the partner antibiotic's lactation guidance.
renal: Sulbactam is eliminated largely unchanged by the kidneys, and its half-life is prolonged in renal impairment. The dosing interval of the combination should be lengthened according to creatinine clearance (e.g. every 6-8 hours for moderate impairment, every 12-24 hours for severe impairment); both sulbactam and the partner are removed by hemodialysis, so dose after dialysis.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for sulbactam in hepatic impairment, but monitor hepatic function during therapy, especially with the partner beta-lactam, as transient elevations of liver enzymes can occur.

major: Probenecid - reduces renal tubular secretion of sulbactam and the partner beta-lactam, raising and prolonging serum levels
moderate: Allopurinol - increased incidence of skin rash with aminopenicillin combinations
Bacteriostatic antibiotics - may antagonize the bactericidal effect of the beta-lactam partner
Combined oral contraceptives - reduced efficacy possible with the partner aminopenicillin
minor: Aminoglycosides - physically incompatible if mixed in the same solution (administer separately)
interactions.diagnostics: Ampicillin combinations may cause false-positive urinary glucose with copper-reduction (non-enzymatic) tests

serious: Severe cutaneous reactions (e.g. Stevens-Johnson syndrome) - rare

monitoring: Renal function (and dose-interval adjustment) with prolonged or high-dose therapy
Complete blood count with prolonged therapy
Signs of hypersensitivity and C. difficile-associated diarrhea
counsel: This medicine is given by injection or drip together with another antibiotic
Tell your clinician about any penicillin or other antibiotic allergy
Report any rash, swelling, breathing difficulty, or severe or bloody diarrhea promptly
Complete the full prescribed course even if you feel better
pk: Therapeutic plasma levels achieved rapidly after IV/IM administration
Peak serum concentration shortly after IV; about 1 hour after IM injection
Approximately 1 hour in normal renal function (prolonged in renal impairment)
Largely (about 75-85%) excreted unchanged in the urine within 8 hours; parallels the partner penicillin
Store the combination powder for injection per the product label, typically below 25-30 C; use reconstituted solution promptly
pearls: Not FDA-approved as a single agent - sulbactam is licensed only in fixed-dose combinations (e.g. ampicillin/sulbactam; cefoperazone/sulbactam outside the US). This record is based on EMA/SmPC and BNF data for those combinations.
Has little antibacterial activity alone; its role is to inactivate beta-lactamases and protect the partner antibiotic
Possesses intrinsic activity against Acinetobacter baumannii and is used (often high-dose) in multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter infections
Cross-reacts with penicillin allergy - share full beta-lactam allergy history before use
Renally eliminated - lengthen the dosing interval in renal impairment and dose after hemodialysis
missed: Not applicable in most settings - sulbactam is given as scheduled parenteral doses (with its partner antibiotic) by healthcare staff. If a scheduled dose is delayed, give it as soon as possible and resume the regular interval; do not double the dose.
overdose: Limited information exists on sulbactam overdose. High serum concentrations of beta-lactams/beta-lactamase inhibitors, particularly in renal impairment, may produce neurological effects including seizures. Management is supportive; both sulbactam and its usual penicillin partner are removed by hemodialysis, which can be used to lower serum concentrations in serious overdose with renal failure.
